newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Britain warns EU it may block beef imports.
newsitem.headline: Britain warns EU it may block beef imports.

text.p: British Farm Minister Jack Cunningham warned fellow European Union ministers on Tuesday to follow scientific advice on mad cow disease controls or face a ban on their beef exports to Britain.

The European Commission, acting on advice from the World Health Organisation (WHO), last week proposed to ban the brains, eyes and spinal cord of cattle, sheep and goats more than 12 months old from human and animal food.
"I reiterated firmly and clearly our position that if they don't act by July 22 I will take unilateral action," Cunningham told reporters during an EU farm ministers' meeting.
Although Britain warned on June 5 that it might take such action unless controls were tightened across the EU, this was the first time the warning had been delivered directly.
"If they don't act it will be in total defiance...of sound scientific advice," Cunningham said.
"Colleagues can't have it both ways. They can't require me to adhere to clear scientific advice and for them to "cop-out" when the scientific advice applies to them," he added.
It means that the specified risk material (SRM) will have to be removed, he said.
Germany and Belgium raised objections, saying that the BSE risk varied among member states and that safety rules should be adjusted accordingly.

But EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler responded that no minister could be certain that neither bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) nor scrapie -- a similar brain-wasting disease in sheep -- existed in their country.
"Removal of SRM will cost money but it is a reasonable price to pay to protect public health," he said.
Fischler also urged Britain to refrain from taking unilateral action as this could undermine the EU beef market.
About 20 percent of beef consumed in Britain is imported, amounting to an estimated 160,000 tonnes this year.

Industry sources said that most of the beef is imported from Ireland which takes the bones out of the meat and respects the tough British food safety standards. Imports of Dutch and German beef were also mostly deboned.
Last December, farm ministers rejected a similar proposal to ban risky cattle parts, arguing it was an unnecessary cost as their countries were virtually free of BSE and scrapie.
Infected meat and bonemeal, containing the risky organs and mixed into cattle and sheep feed, is believed to be the main cause of BSE.
